Chunk over valid sequence positions, keeping all 33 candidates per position; splitting the softmax denominator changes the objective. For N valid positions, use each chunk’s cross-entropy sum divided by N, including the smaller final chunk. This preserves the global mean-loss gradient, up to floating-point differences. Accumulating differentiable chunk losses before one backward retains every chunk’s graph and saved candidate embeddings; smaller temporary logits alone do not bound retained memory. See [PyTorch autograd mechanics](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/notes/autograd.html).

An implementable strategy: zero gradients once; compute encoder features H; create Z = H.detach().requires_grad_(True). For each position chunk, freshly look up its candidate embeddings, compute logits from Z, and immediately backward its normalized loss. This accumulates Z.grad and scoring-parameter gradients while releasing each scoring graph. Finally call H.backward(Z.grad), then clip gradients and step once. With tied item embeddings, leave candidate lookups attached: their direct scoring gradients must accumulate with the encoder’s embedding gradients. Do not precompute graph-connected candidate embeddings across chunks. Peak memory comprises the retained encoder graph, features/feature gradients, parameter gradients, and one candidate chunk. This construction follows PyTorch’s documented [gradient accumulation and vector-Jacobian backward](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.autograd.backward.html).

Activation checkpointing can additionally reduce encoder activations by recomputing segments; use use_reentrant=False and preserve_rng_state=True for matching dropout during replay. Alternatively, compute features without gradients, accumulate feature/scorer gradients, then recompute the encoder for its backward, restoring encoder RNG state so dropout matches the original pass. Keep weights and sampled candidates fixed; account for mutable buffers. Full encoder recomputation per scoring chunk costs more compute. The detached-feature strategy requires only one encoder forward/backward and naturally reuses its dropout realization. See [checkpointing documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/utils/checkpoint.html).
